title: Digital twin concepts and transport fundamentals
goals: Define a digital twin and name its three parts
Tell a digital model, shadow and twin apart by their data flows
Match transport decisions to the time scales a twin must serve
reading:
From product engineering to roads

The digital twin idea comes from product lifecycle management. Michael Grieves described it in 2002 as a physical product, a virtual product and the data that ties them together. NASA and the US Air Force then used the term for aircraft and spacecraft: a simulation of one specific, as-built vehicle, updated with its own sensor data and history, so engineers could predict how that particular vehicle would age. Factories adopted twins in the 2010s, and cities and infrastructure followed, with initiatives such as Virtual Singapore and the UK's Gemini Principles (2018).

The three parts, in transport terms

  • Physical system: a corridor, a bus network, a bridge, a port terminal, including the people using it.
  • Virtual replica: the models that represent its current state: a traffic simulation, a prediction model, a structural model, a 3D geometry.
  • Connection: data from detectors, cameras, GPS and ticketing flowing in; signal plans, holding instructions, speed limits or work orders flowing out.

Model, shadow, twin

Kritzinger et al. (2018) classify systems by how data moves. A digital model is updated by hand. A digital shadow receives data automatically, but decisions go back through people. A digital twin exchanges data automatically in both directions. Reviews of transport research keep finding that many systems described as twins are really shadows. That is not a failure: a shadow is a sensible first stage. It only becomes a problem when the label promises more than the system does.

Why transport is different

A machine on a factory floor has one owner, a fixed design and well-instrumented parts. A transport system is open: demand changes with weather, events and prices; drivers and passengers adapt to every intervention; one journey crosses assets owned by a city, a highway agency, a transit operator and private fleets. Assets last for decades, so a twin must handle both second-by-second operations and very slow deterioration.

Time scales drive design

DecisionTime scaleTypical data
Signal timingSecondsQueues and arrivals per approach
Incident responseMinutesSpeeds, camera feeds, incident reports
Bus holdingMinutesVehicle positions and headways
Pavement repairWeeks to yearsRoughness, cracking, loading
New transit lineYearsTravel demand, land use

A twin that serves signal control needs fresh data every second and a fast model. A pavement twin can update weekly but must hold decades of history. Trying to serve every decision with one twin usually produces a costly platform that serves none of them well.

Three questions to ask about any “twin”

  1. Which data flows in automatically, and how often?
  2. Which decision does it change, and who or what acts on it?
  3. How is its accuracy measured against reality?

audio.title: Why a live picture is not enough
audio.script:
Imagine you run the traffic control room for a busy city. On the wall there is a beautiful live map. Every road glows green, yellow or red, updated every minute from phone and vehicle data. Is that a digital twin? Most people would say yes. By the definition used in this course, it is not. It is a digital shadow.
The map tells you what is happening. It does not tell you what will happen in fifteen minutes, it cannot test what would happen if you changed the signal plan, and it does not act. A person still has to notice the problem, decide, and pick up the phone.
A digital twin closes that loop. It takes the live data, estimates the state of the whole network, predicts where the queue is heading, tries a few options in simulation, and sends the best one back to the signals, within limits that engineers have agreed in advance.
Here is the second idea to take away. The twin is defined by its decision, not by its technology. A twin for signal timing must think in seconds. A twin for bridge maintenance thinks in months and years. They might share a database, but their sensors, models and update speeds are completely different.
So when someone shows you a digital twin, ask three things. What flows in automatically, and how often? What decision does it change, and who acts on it? And how do they know it is accurate? Those three questions will carry you through the whole course.

slides.title: Digital twin concepts
slides.notes: Welcome to module one. In the next two minutes we will define a digital twin, separate it from things that only look like one, and see why transport is both a natural fit and a hard case.

slides.title: Three parts and a loop
slides.notes: A digital twin has three parts: a physical system, a virtual replica of it, and the connection between them. Data flows in from the road, and decisions flow back out. Without that two-way connection, you only have a model.

slides.title: Model, shadow or twin?
slides.notes: Kritzinger and colleagues give a simple test. A model has no automatic data flow. A shadow receives live data, but people act on it by hand. Only when data flows automatically in both directions do we call it a twin.

slides.title: Five questions a twin answers
slides.notes: A dashboard answers the first question. A full twin climbs all five: it monitors, diagnoses, predicts, tests options, and finally acts. Each step needs more trust in the data and the models.

slides.title: Why transport is a hard case
slides.notes: Transport is harder than a factory. The system is open, full of human behaviour, spread across many owners, and its decisions run from a signal change in seconds to a new metro line over decades.

slides.title: Start with the decision
slides.notes: So every good twin starts with one decision. The decision sets the clock, and the clock sets which data, which model detail, and which update speed you need. That is the thread for the rest of the course.

title: Architecture and cyber-physical systems
goals: Describe a transport twin as a cyber-physical system
Lay out a layered reference architecture and its data paths
Explain co-simulation, the digital thread, and edge versus cloud choices
reading:
Transport as a cyber-physical system

A cyber-physical system (CPS) tightly couples computation with a physical process through sensors and actuators. Transport cyber-physical systems (TCPS) include connected vehicles, adaptive signals, ramp meters and train control. A digital twin is the part of such a system that keeps a synchronised virtual representation and uses it to reason about the future. This framing matters because CPS engineering brings requirements that pure data projects ignore: deadlines, fail-safe behaviour, certification and cyber security.

A reference architecture

LayerResponsibilityDesign concerns
PhysicalThe road, vehicles, signals, peopleWhat can be observed and influenced
SensingDetect and measureCoverage, accuracy, maintenance
Data platformIngest, store, clean, linkTimestamps, identifiers, quality flags
ModelsEstimate, predict, simulateFidelity, run time, validation
ServicesTurn results into decisionsRules, optimisation, safety limits
InterfacesOperators, planners, public, other systemsExplanation, standards, access control

ISO 23247, written for manufacturing twins, uses a similar split into observable elements, device communication, the twin core and the user domain; transport projects often borrow it. The UK Gemini Principles add governance values: a twin should have a clear purpose, be trustworthy (secure, open where possible, of known quality) and work as part of a federation.

Data paths and timing

Every twin has at least two paths. The fast path carries live data to models and decisions within the decision's deadline, for example under two seconds for signal control. The slow path stores history for calibration, learning and reporting. Mixing them is a common mistake: a heavy analytics query should never delay a control decision. Designers therefore set a latency budget for each step of the fast path and monitor it in operation.

Co-simulation and model exchange

Realistic twins combine specialised models: traffic flow, vehicle dynamics, communication networks, energy use. Co-simulation runs them together, exchanging state at agreed time steps. The Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI) is a widely used standard for packaging models so that tools can exchange them. In this course you will use TraCI, SUMO's interface, which lets a Python program step the simulation and read or change any object.

The digital thread

For infrastructure, the twin also needs the history of each asset: design models, construction records, inspections and repairs. The digital thread is the linked record that carries this information through the lifecycle, so that a maintenance decision in year 30 can use the as-built geometry from year 1.

Edge, cloud and resilience

Edge computing processes data near the source: a camera box that outputs vehicle counts instead of video, or a controller that keeps running its normal plan if the twin goes silent. Cloud or data-centre computing hosts history, simulation and dashboards. The safe rule is that the physical system must stay safe if any upper layer fails.

audio.title: The fast path and the slow path
audio.script:
Here is a design rule that will save you from many painful projects. Every digital twin has a fast path and a slow path, and they must never get in each other's way.
The fast path is the loop that makes decisions. Data leaves a camera or a loop detector, travels to the platform, updates the model, the model recommends an action, and the action reaches the signal controller. For a traffic signal, all of that might have to happen in under two seconds. So every step gets a budget: a few hundred milliseconds for detection, a few hundred for the network, and so on. If the total is longer than the decision allows, the twin is too slow, however clever it is.
The slow path is everything else: storing years of history, recalibrating the model each night, training a new prediction model, producing a monthly report. These jobs are heavy and they can wait.
Problems start when the two share resources without limits. Someone runs a big analytics query, the database slows down, and the live loop misses its deadline. That is why mature architectures separate them, and why the physical system must always fall back to safe behaviour on its own.
The second idea from this module is that architecture is a set of answers, not a set of products. What is the purpose? How much fidelity do we need? How often must it update? How much delay can we accept? Who owns each layer? Write those answers down first. Then choose the tools.

slides.title: Architecture
slides.notes: Module two is about architecture: how sensors, data, models and decisions fit together, and the design choices that make a twin fast, reliable and safe.

slides.title: A cyber-physical system
slides.notes: A transport twin is a cyber-physical system. Computers and the physical road form one loop. That means timing and safety matter as much as model accuracy: a late decision can be as bad as a wrong one.

slides.title: Layered architecture
slides.notes: Most twins can be drawn as layers: the physical system, sensing, a data platform, models, services that turn results into decisions, and interfaces for people. A feedback path runs from the services back to the physical layer.

slides.title: Edge or cloud?
slides.notes: Where should computation run? Video analytics and safety logic belong at the edge, close to the camera and the signal. History, heavy simulation and city-wide analytics fit the cloud or a data centre. Most real twins use both.

slides.title: Co-simulation and the digital thread
slides.notes: No single simulator does everything, so twins couple several, for example SUMO for traffic and CARLA for vehicles. The digital thread is the record that links design, construction and operating data for each asset.

slides.title: Five design questions
slides.notes: Before choosing products, answer five questions: what is the purpose, how much fidelity is needed, how often must it update, how much delay is acceptable, and who owns each layer. The architecture follows from the answers.

title: Static inputs: reality capture, GIS and BIM
goals: Choose a reality-capture method for a transport asset
Turn point clouds and GIS data into a network model
Use BIM and IFC 4.3 as the geometric backbone of an asset twin
reading:
Why static inputs matter

Live data only makes sense on top of an accurate description of the network: where the lanes are, which turns are allowed, where the detectors and cameras sit, how high a bridge deck is. Errors here propagate everywhere. A missing turn lane, for example, will make a calibrated model look wrong no matter how good the detectors are.

Reality-capture methods

MethodTypical useStrengthsLimits
Terrestrial laser scanningBridges, junctions, tunnelsVery high detail and accuracySlow; many set-ups
Mobile laser scanningRoad and rail corridorsKilometres per hour at traffic speedCostly equipment, occlusions
Airborne lidarRegions, terrainWide coverageLower detail on small features
UAV photogrammetrySites, structures, inspectionsCheap, flexible, coloured modelsLight, weather, flight rules

Point clouds are stored in formats such as LAS/LAZ or E57. Processing steps are registration (aligning scans), georeferencing (tying them to survey control points), classification (ground, road, vegetation, structures), and feature extraction. Tools range from open-source CloudCompare to commercial suites.

From geometry to a traffic network

A traffic simulator needs a topological network: nodes (junctions), links (road segments), lanes with widths and speeds, connections between lanes (which turns are allowed), signal programmes, and detectors. Sources include OpenStreetMap, agency GIS layers, survey data and design drawings. SUMO's netconvert, for example, imports OpenStreetMap or plain XML and builds lanes, connections and default signal plans, which engineers then correct.

Demand

Demand is usually described as an origin–destination (OD) matrix: trips between every pair of zones, by time period. It comes from household surveys, census commuting data, mobile-phone data, and, crucially, adjustment against traffic counts (module 7). For public transport, schedules in GTFS give the supply side.

BIM and open standards

Building information modelling (BIM) gives each asset structured geometry and properties. IFC 4.3, published as ISO 16739-1:2024, extended IFC to infrastructure: alignments, road and rail elements, bridges. CityGML (OGC) represents city objects at levels of detail from footprints to full 3D. ASAM OpenDRIVE describes lane-level road networks for driving and automated-vehicle simulators. Using these formats prevents lock-in and lets the twin outlive any single software product.

Practical advice

  • Agree one coordinate reference system and height datum for the whole project.
  • Specify accuracy by use: lane-level traffic modelling needs decimetres; bridge deformation needs millimetres.
  • Record when and how each dataset was captured; geometry changes after road works.

audio.title: Garbage in, confident garbage out
audio.script:
There is an old saying in computing: garbage in, garbage out. Digital twins have a worse version. Garbage in, confident garbage out. A twin built on the wrong geometry will still produce smooth, convincing numbers. They will just be wrong.
Here is a real pattern from traffic modelling. A team calibrates a corridor model for weeks. The counts never match on one approach. Eventually someone visits the site and finds a short right-turn lane that was added two years ago and never made it into the map. One missing lane, weeks of wasted effort.
That is why this module spends time on static inputs. Laser scanning and drone photogrammetry can capture a corridor or a bridge in great detail. But the raw points are only the start. They have to be aligned, tied to survey control, classified, and turned into the objects a model understands: lanes, turns, signals, kerbs, bridge girders.
Two pieces of advice. First, decide the accuracy you need from the decision, not from the equipment brochure. Lane-level traffic modelling is happy with a few decimetres. Monitoring bridge deformation needs millimetres. Second, use open formats. IFC 4.3 for roads, rail and bridges, CityGML for the city, OpenDRIVE for driving simulators. Software products come and go. Your survey data should not have to.

slides.t: Network models need more than geometry

slides.title: Static inputs
slides.notes: Module three covers static inputs: the geometry and structure of the network that a twin needs before any live data can make sense.

slides.title: Ways to capture reality
slides.notes: Reality capture comes in two families. Laser scanning, from a tripod, a vehicle or an aircraft, measures millions of points directly. Photogrammetry rebuilds 3D shape from overlapping drone photos. Accuracy, cost and coverage decide which to use.

slides.title: From points to a model
slides.notes: Raw point clouds are only the start. They are registered into one coordinate system, classified into road, kerb, vegetation and structures, and then features such as lane edges and signs are extracted into a network or a BIM model.

slides.title: Network models need more than geometry
slides.notes: A traffic model needs more than geometry. It needs nodes, links, lanes and the turns allowed between them, the signal programmes, and the demand: how many trips travel between each pair of zones.

slides.title: BIM, IFC 4.3 and CityGML
slides.notes: Open standards keep this data usable. IFC 4.3 extends building information modelling to roads, rail and bridges. CityGML describes city objects at different levels of detail. OpenDRIVE describes lane-level roads for driving simulators.

slides.title: Rule of thumb
slides.notes: Capture is expensive, so plan it to serve many uses. Agree the coordinate system, the accuracy you need and the output formats before anyone goes on site.

title: Dynamic inputs: sensors and data standards
goals: Compare the main transport sensors and their blind spots
Judge data quality on four dimensions
Name the standards for exchanging live transport data
reading:
The main sources

SourceMeasuresUpdateWatch out for
Inductive loopsCounts, occupancy; speed with paired loops20 s–5 min aggregatesFailures go unnoticed; one point only
Radar / microwaveCounts and speed per laneSeconds–minutesMounting and calibration
Video with computer visionClasses, turning movements, queues, conflictsPer frameNight, rain, glare, occlusion, privacy
Bluetooth / Wi-Fi re-identificationTravel time between readersPer matchSmall, changing sample; must hash identifiers
Probe GPS (floating car data)Link speeds, travel times1–5 minSample bias, licence terms
Bus AVL / APCPositions, passenger loads10–30 sFeed gaps, stop matching
Fare cardsBoardings; trips inferredPer tapAlightings often missing
Connected vehicles (V2X)Vehicle state; signal phase messagesUp to 10 HzLow penetration
Structural and environmental sensorsStrain, vibration, air qualitySeconds–hoursPower, drift, maintenance

Data quality

Four dimensions cover most problems. Completeness: missing intervals, failed detectors. Accuracy: miscounts, position errors. Timeliness: delay between the event and its arrival. Consistency: whether sources agree, for example loop counts against camera counts on the same lane. Good twins attach a quality flag to every value and keep the raw data so that cleaning can be redone.

Cleaning and imputation

Typical steps: remove impossible values (speeds above a plausible limit, occupancy over 100%), detect stuck detectors (identical values for hours), fill short gaps from neighbours or historical patterns, and mark long gaps rather than inventing data. Imputed values must be flagged so that calibration does not treat them as observations.

Fusion

Fusion can be complementary (sources cover different places or quantities), competitive (sources measure the same thing and are combined to reduce error) or cooperative (sources together reveal something neither can alone, such as travel time from two cameras matching vehicles). Kalman filters and their variants are the classic tools; module 6 returns to them.

Standards

  • GTFS (schedules) and GTFS-Realtime (vehicle positions, trip updates, alerts) are the most common public-transport formats worldwide.
  • SIRI and NeTEx are the European CEN standards for real-time and network data.
  • DATEX II exchanges road traffic and travel information between European operators.
  • SAE J2735 defines connected-vehicle messages such as the basic safety message and signal phase and timing (SPaT).
  • NGSI-LD (ETSI) is the context-information API used by FIWARE platforms; the OGC SensorThings API is another open option for IoT observations.

Privacy

Movement data is personal data. Aggregate where you can, hash or rotate device identifiers, process video at the edge and discard frames, and follow the law that applies, such as the EU GDPR or Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law.

audio.title: The camera that could not see in the rain
audio.script:
Let's talk about sensors through a story you will meet again in the SUMO lab. A city installs cameras at a junction because cameras see so much more than loops. They can classify vehicles, count turning movements and measure the whole queue. The twin is fed from the cameras, and on sunny afternoons it performs beautifully.
Then the rainy season arrives. Detection drops at night. Long queues hide cars behind other cars. The twin starts to underestimate demand on one approach, gives it less green, and the queue grows. Nobody notices for a week, because the dashboard still looks smooth.
What went wrong was not the camera. It was the assumption that one source is enough. Every sensor has a blind spot. Loops are reliable but see one point. Probe GPS covers the network but samples only some vehicles. Cameras are rich but sensitive to light, weather and occlusion.
So the habits to build are these. Judge each feed on completeness, accuracy, timeliness and consistency. Attach a quality flag to every value. Compare sources against each other continuously, for example camera counts against loop counts on the same lane, and raise an alarm when they drift apart. And fuse sources so that each covers another's weakness.
Finally, remember that much of this data describes people. Aggregate it, hash identifiers, keep video at the edge, and follow the privacy law where you work.

Positions and speeds reported by a sample of vehicles or phones.

slides.t: Every source has a blind spot

slides.title: Dynamic inputs
slides.notes: Module four is about dynamic inputs: the sensors and data feeds that keep a twin in step with reality, and the standards that let systems share them.

slides.title: Point or network?
slides.notes: Sensors fall into two groups. Point sensors, like loops, radar and cameras, are accurate but only see one place. Network sources, like probe GPS and bus locations, cover the whole city but only sample some of the vehicles.

slides.title: Every source has a blind spot
slides.notes: Every source has a blind spot. Loops see one point. Cameras struggle with darkness, rain and hidden vehicles. Probe data is biased toward certain vehicles. Connected-vehicle messages are still rare. That is why twins fuse several sources.

slides.title: Four dimensions of data quality
slides.notes: Judge every feed on four dimensions: completeness, accuracy, timeliness and consistency. A feed that is accurate but arrives five minutes late is useless for signal control, and perfectly fine for planning.

slides.title: Standards for live data
slides.notes: Standards let systems share data without custom code. GTFS-Realtime and SIRI carry live public transport data. DATEX II carries road traffic information in Europe. SAE J2735 defines connected-vehicle messages. NGSI-LD is used by smart city platforms.

slides.title: Fusion
slides.notes: The goal is fusion: combining sources so that each covers another's blind spot. A camera that sees the queue plus a loop that counts reliably gives a better picture than either alone.

title: Data platforms, cloud and interoperability
goals: Choose between streaming and batch processing
Pick storage for time series, geometry and context
Explain the four levels of interoperability
reading:
Moving data

Sensors and edge devices usually publish small messages. MQTT is a lightweight publish–subscribe protocol well suited to many small devices; brokers include Eclipse Mosquitto and EMQX. Apache Kafka is a distributed log built for very high volumes and replay: consumers can reread past messages, which is valuable when a model must be rerun. Many platforms use MQTT at the edge and Kafka in the core.

Processing

Stream processing (for example Apache Flink, Kafka Streams or simple Python consumers) cleans, aggregates and joins data as it arrives: converting 20-second loop data to 1-minute flows, matching bus positions to stops, flagging failed detectors. Batch processing runs over history: nightly calibration, model training, monthly performance reports. Keeping them separate protects the live loop.

Storage

NeedTypical storeExample query
Sensor historyTimescaleDB, InfluxDBAverage flow on lane 2 every 15 min last March
Networks and assetsPostgreSQL + PostGISAll detectors within 200 m of junction J2
Live state of objectsNGSI-LD context broker, twin graph (Eclipse Ditto, Azure Digital Twins)Current queue and phase at every junction
Raw archiveObject storage with Parquet filesReprocess all camera detections from 2025

Interoperability

Interoperability works at four levels. Technical: network access and protocols. Syntactic: shared formats such as JSON, XML, GTFS or DATEX II. Semantic: shared meaning, achieved with data models and vocabularies such as Transmodel for public transport, the FIWARE Smart Data Models, or ontologies. Organisational: agreements, licences and responsibilities. Technical and syntactic problems are solved in days; semantic and organisational ones take months and decide whether a federation of twins can exist.

Cloud, on premises or both

Cloud platforms offer managed brokers, databases and twin services (for example Azure Digital Twins and AWS IoT TwinMaker), which speed up pilots. On-premises deployment gives control over data location and cost at scale. Hybrid designs are common: edge devices at the roadside, operational systems on premises, analytics and archives in the cloud. Check where personal data is stored and processed against local law.

Operating the platform

A twin is software that must run every day. Containerisation (Docker), orchestration (Kubernetes), monitoring of message rates and latency (Prometheus and Grafana), access control (for example Keycloak) and versioned deployments are not extras; they are what lets a pilot become a service.

audio.title: Two systems that both said 'stop'
audio.script:
Here is a small story about interoperability. A city connected its bus operator's system to its traffic signal system so that late buses could get extra green. The connection worked on the first day. The messages arrived, the formats parsed, everything looked fine. And nothing improved.
The problem was the word 'stop'. In the bus system, a stop was a pole on the pavement, with an identifier the operator invented. In the signal system, the relevant thing was the approach lane before the junction. Nobody had agreed how one mapped to the other, so the priority requests pointed at the wrong places.
That is the difference between syntactic and semantic interoperability. Syntactic means both systems can read the message. Semantic means they agree on what it means. Shared data models, such as Transmodel for public transport or the FIWARE smart data models, exist to solve exactly this.
And there is a fourth level above that: organisational. Are the two agencies allowed to share the data, who maintains the mapping when a stop moves, and who is responsible when it is wrong? In practice, that level takes the longest.
The technical choices in this module, MQTT, Kafka, time-series and spatial databases, context brokers, are well understood. Choose them sensibly, keep the live path separate from history, and spend your real effort on meaning and agreements. That is what lets your twin join a federation later.

Distributed event log for high-volume streaming with replay.
Service holding the current state of entities, for example via NGSI-LD.
Systems agree on what the data means, not just its format.
Columnar file format for efficient archives and analytics.

slides.t: The right store for each job

slides.title: Data platforms
slides.notes: Module five looks at the data platform: how a twin moves, stores and shares data, and how it stays interoperable with other systems.

slides.title: A typical data path
slides.notes: A typical path: sensors publish messages to a broker such as MQTT or Kafka, a stream processor cleans and aggregates them, results land in time-series and spatial databases, and APIs expose them to models and users.

slides.title: Streaming or batch?
slides.notes: Streaming handles data as it arrives and keeps the live state. Batch processing runs over history, for calibration, learning and reports. Twins need both, connected but separated.

slides.title: The right store for each job
slides.notes: Use the right store for each job: a time-series database for sensor history, a spatial database for networks and assets, a context broker or twin graph for the live state of each object, and cheap object storage for the raw archive.

slides.title: Four levels of interoperability
slides.notes: Interoperability has four levels. Technical: can the systems connect. Syntactic: can they parse the format. Semantic: does a 'stop' or a 'link' mean the same thing to both. Organisational: are they allowed to share. Most projects fail at the last two.

slides.title: Design for federation
slides.notes: Design for federation from the start. Keep ownership of your data, expose it through open APIs and shared vocabularies, and your twin can connect to neighbours' twins later without being rebuilt.

title: Traffic state estimation and AI prediction
goals: Explain traffic state estimation as data assimilation
Compare model-based, data-driven and hybrid prediction
Evaluate predictions honestly with the right metrics
reading:
The estimation problem

Detectors cover a small share of a network; probe vehicles are a sample. Traffic state estimation (TSE) reconstructs density, speed and flow on every link from these sparse observations. It is a data-assimilation problem: a model propagates the state forward in time, and observations correct it. The classic model is the Lighthill–Whitham–Richards (LWR) conservation law, often discretised as Daganzo's cell transmission model. Filters such as the Kalman filter, the extended and ensemble Kalman filters, and particle filters do the blending.

Prediction approaches

FamilyExamplesStrengthsWeaknesses
Naive baselinesLast value, historical average for the time of dayHard to beat at short horizonsMiss incidents
StatisticalARIMA, Kalman-basedSimple, interpretableStruggle with network effects
Machine learningk-nearest neighbours, gradient boostingFlexible, fastFeature engineering
Deep learningLSTM; graph neural networks such as STGCN, DCRNN, Graph WaveNetCapture spatial and temporal patternsData-hungry, opaque
Model-basedCell transmission with data assimilation; simulationPhysically consistent, handles new situationsCalibration effort
Hybrid / physics-informedNeural networks with conservation constraints; residual learningLess data, plausible outputsMore complex to build

Evaluation

Use mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), reported separately for each horizon (for example 5, 15, 30 and 60 minutes). Always include naive baselines; many published gains over them are small at short horizons. Split data by time, not randomly, to avoid leakage: training on Tuesday afternoon and testing on the same Tuesday morning tells you little. Test separately on incident periods and on months not seen in training. Public benchmarks such as METR-LA and PEMS-BAY make comparisons possible, but they are freeway data; urban networks with signals behave differently.

Computer vision for estimation

Cameras feed estimation directly: detectors such as YOLO find vehicles, trackers such as ByteTrack follow them across frames, and a homography maps image positions to road coordinates. The same techniques detect pavement cracks and inspect bridges (module 9). Detection rates fall with darkness, weather and occlusion, which must be modelled rather than ignored, as the camera twin in module 8 shows.

From estimate to decision

A prediction is useful only if its horizon exceeds the time needed to compute it and act. For signals, a 30-second look-ahead may be enough; for incident management, 15 to 30 minutes; for event planning, days. Uncertainty matters too: a forecast with a range lets operators judge risk, while a single number invites false confidence.

audio.title: Beating yesterday at the same time
audio.script:
Here is a humbling exercise for anyone building traffic prediction models. Before you train anything clever, write down the simplest possible forecast: tomorrow at eight fifteen, traffic will look like it did on the same weekday at eight fifteen, averaged over the last few weeks. Then measure how wrong that is.
You will often find that this naive baseline is very hard to beat, especially for short horizons on normal days. Many impressive-looking deep learning results shrink when compared with it properly.
So where do advanced models earn their keep? In three places. First, at longer horizons, where the state of the whole network matters, and graph neural networks can learn how congestion spreads along roads. Second, on unusual days: incidents, events, weather. And third, in filling gaps, where a physical model, combined with sparse sensors through a Kalman filter, can estimate speeds on roads that have no sensors at all.
Two habits will keep you honest. Split your data by time, never randomly, so the model is always tested on a future it has not seen. And report error by horizon and by condition: normal days, incident days, new months.
Last point. A forecast has to arrive before the decision. If your model predicts the next five minutes but takes six minutes to run, it is a history book. Check the clock as carefully as the accuracy.

slides.notes: Module six turns sparse sensor data into a full picture of the network, now and in the near future.

slides.title: Traffic state estimation
slides.notes: Traffic state estimation is like weather forecasting. A few detectors and probe vehicles give sparse observations. A flow model fills the gaps, and a filter, such as a Kalman filter, blends the two into speeds and densities on every link.

slides.title: Two families of prediction
slides.notes: Prediction comes in two families. Model-based methods use flow physics and explain themselves, but need calibration. Data-driven methods, such as LSTMs and graph neural networks, learn patterns from history but need large clean datasets.

slides.title: Hybrid and physics-informed
slides.notes: Hybrid and physics-informed approaches combine both: a network learns what the physical model gets wrong, or is trained to respect conservation of vehicles. They need less data and produce fewer impossible answers.

slides.title: Evaluate honestly
slides.notes: Evaluate honestly. Report errors by forecast horizon, always compare with simple baselines such as yesterday at the same time, and test on incidents and on months the model never saw.

slides.title: Remember
slides.notes: And remember: a forecast is only useful if it arrives in time. The prediction horizon must be longer than the time it takes to compute it and act on it.

title: Simulation I: building and calibrating a model
goals: Choose macroscopic, mesoscopic or microscopic simulation
Build a SUMO network with demand, signals and detectors
Calibrate and validate with GEH and travel times across several seeds
reading:
Levels of detail

LevelRepresentsTypical useTools
MacroscopicFlow, density and speed on linksRegional strategy, fast predictionPTV Visum, cell transmission models
MesoscopicVehicles or platoons moving through link queuesCity-wide dynamic assignmentAimsun meso, MATSim
MicroscopicEach vehicle with car-following and lane-changingCorridors, junctions, signals, rampsSUMO, PTV Vissim, Aimsun micro

Behaviour models

Car-following models set each driver's speed from the gap and speed difference to the vehicle ahead. SUMO's default is a variant of Krauss's safe-speed model; the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) and Gipps' model are widely used alternatives; Vissim uses Wiedemann's psycho-physical model. Lane-changing models decide when drivers change lanes for routing, speed or cooperation. Route choice can be fixed, or assigned dynamically so that drivers react to congestion.

Building the model in SUMO

  1. Network: netconvert imports OpenStreetMap or plain XML, creates lanes, connections and default signal programmes. Check every junction in netedit.
  2. Demand: flows or trips between edges or zones; duarouter or SUMO itself computes routes. randomTrips.py is useful for testing, not for calibrated studies.
  3. Control: fixed-time or actuated signal programmes, priority rules, public-transport stops.
  4. Detectors and outputs: induction loops (E1) and lane-area detectors (E2) mirror real sensors; tripinfo, summary and edge outputs give performance measures.

Calibration

Calibration usually starts with demand, because most errors come from wrong OD flows rather than wrong driver parameters. Adjust demand to match counts (OD matrix estimation), then tune behaviour parameters (for example minimum gap, reaction time, imperfection) to match speeds and queue lengths. The GEH statistic compares modelled flow M with counted flow C:

GEH = √( 2 (M − C)² / (M + C) )

UK guidance (DMRB and TAG unit M3.1) looks for GEH below 5 on at least 85% of counted links, and modelled travel times within 15% of observed on at least 85% of routes.

Validation and randomness

Validate on days not used for calibration. Because microsimulation is stochastic, run several random seeds and report the mean and spread; agencies often require a minimum number of runs. Never tune a controller and evaluate it on the same seeds. In building this course's SUMO lab, a twin controller tuned on one seed looked better than actuated control, then lost to it on five fresh seeds: a textbook case of overfitting.

Common mistakes

  • Missing or wrong turn lanes and signal programmes.
  • Demand that ignores the hour-by-hour profile.
  • Calibrating to counts only, ignoring speeds and queues.
  • Reporting one run.

audio.title: The model that was tuned to one day
audio.script:
This module has a confession in it. While building the SUMO lab for this course, we tuned a digital twin controller on one random seed of the simulation. On that seed it was the clear winner, with less delay than SUMO's own actuated signals. Then we ran five fresh seeds that the controller had never seen. It lost. Not by a little.
Nothing was broken. The controller had simply learned the quirks of one particular day of simulated traffic. That is overfitting, and it is the most common way that simulation studies mislead people, including the people who wrote them.
The cure is a discipline you will use throughout this course. Calibrate on one set of data and validate on another. In practice that means tuning on some days or seeds, and reporting results only on days or seeds you kept aside. It also means running several seeds and showing the range, not just one tidy number.
Calibration itself has an order. Start with demand, because most errors come from wrong origin and destination flows, not from driver behaviour. Use the GEH statistic to compare modelled and counted flows, aiming for GEH below five on most links. Then check speeds, queues and travel times, which counts alone cannot confirm.
A calibrated, validated model is the engine of a twin. Build it carefully, test it honestly, and the rest of the course will rest on something solid.

slides.notes: Module seven builds the engine of the twin: a traffic simulation that is calibrated and validated well enough to be trusted.

slides.title: Choose the zoom level
slides.notes: First choose the zoom level. Macroscopic and mesoscopic models move flows or platoons and suit whole regions. Microscopic models simulate every driver and suit corridors, junctions and signals, at the price of speed and data.

slides.title: Inside a microscopic model
slides.notes: Inside a microscopic model, car-following rules decide how drivers keep their distance. SUMO's default is the Krauss model, Vissim uses Wiedemann. Lane-changing and route choice complete the picture.

slides.title: Building in SUMO
slides.notes: In SUMO the workflow is: build the network with netconvert, generate demand and routes, add detectors, run sumo or sumo-gui, and read the outputs such as trip information and detector counts.

slides.title: Calibrate, then validate
slides.notes: Calibration adjusts demand and parameters until the model matches counts. A common target is GEH below five on at least eighty-five percent of counted links. Then validate on different days, and check travel times too.

slides.title: One run is not a result
slides.notes: Finally, one run is not a result. Simulations are random. Run several seeds, report the mean and the range, and never tune and test on the same seed. In the SUMO lab you will see what happens when you do.

title: Simulation II: a real-time twin with a camera
goals: Connect a controller to SUMO through TraCI
Model camera sensing with realistic flaws
Compare controllers fairly and interpret mixed results
reading:
Connecting a controller with TraCI

TraCI (Traffic Control Interface) lets a Python program start SUMO, advance it step by step, read any object (detectors, vehicles, signals) and change it. libsumo offers the same functions in-process for more speed. The twin in this course runs a loop every simulated second:

traci.simulationStep() → twin.sense() → twin.demand() → decide → traci.trafficlight.setPhase(...)

The twin controller

At each junction the twin estimates demand on the main street and the side street as vehicles queued plus vehicles that will reach the stop line within a short horizon (8 seconds). It switches green when the served approach is empty and the other is waiting, or when the waiting side exceeds twice the served side plus a margin, always respecting minimum and maximum greens and never skipping the yellow. Its edge over local actuated control is network-wide information: it can see a platoon released by the previous junction before it arrives.

The virtual camera

To make sensing realistic, the camera-fed twin never reads SUMO's ground truth. A camera at each junction reports detections with: a 110 m range; detection probability falling from 98% close up to 80% at the edge; occlusion when a nearer car lies on the same line of sight; about 1 m of position noise; speeds estimated from successive noisy positions; and lanes assigned by map matching. In the runs, the camera at J2 detected about 84% of vehicles at low demand, 70% at medium and 56% at high demand, because long queues hide cars.

Results on held-out seeds

Time loss, s per trip (mean of seeds 1–5)LowMediumHigh
Fixed-time (90 s, equal split)45.2136.4198.3
SUMO actuated15.635.0101.0
Twin, detectors17.539.496.1
Twin, cameras20.138.794.7

The twin settings were chosen on separate training seeds (101–103). Both twins reduced stops at every demand level, but cut delay only at high demand. The effect of imperfect sensing was small and mixed for this simple controller: missed cars made it slower to switch, which sometimes helped.

Interpreting mixed results

These results are typical of real projects. Good local actuation is a strong baseline; a twin earns its place when it uses information local control lacks (platoons, network-wide queues, predictions) and when traffic is heavy enough for that information to matter. The honest way to report is by demand level, over several seeds, with the trade-off between stops and delay made explicit.

From here to the street

Module 12 lists the steps to deploy a camera twin: siting and survey, detection and tracking, pixel-to-road homography, streaming, keeping the simulation in step with detections, a safety shell on the signal controller, and weeks of shadow mode before closing the loop.

audio.title: When the twin did not win
audio.script:
This is the module where the twin gets tested, and the results are not a simple victory. That is exactly why they are worth listening to.
We built a three-junction corridor in SUMO and compared four ways of running the signals. Fixed-time, the old way: ninety-second cycles, equal green for everyone. SUMO's actuated control, which extends green while its own detectors keep seeing cars. A digital twin that sees the whole corridor, including platoons coming from the previous junction. And the same twin, but blindfolded a little: it only knows what virtual cameras report, with cars missed, hidden and misplaced.
Fixed-time lost badly everywhere. No surprise. The interesting fight was between actuated control and the twins. On quiet and medium days, actuated control was slightly better at keeping delay down. On busy days, both twins won. And at every level, the twins stopped cars less often.
What about the camera? Its detection rate fell from about eighty-four percent on quiet days to fifty-six percent on busy ones, because queues hide cars. Yet the camera-fed twin did about as well as the perfect one. Missing cars made it a little slower to switch, which sometimes helped.
So the take-away is not 'twins are better'. It is that a twin is limited by two things, what it can see and how it decides, and the only way to know which limit you are hitting is to measure, honestly, across conditions and seeds.

slides.title: The loop, every second
slides.notes: Every simulated second the twin senses the road, estimates queues and arriving vehicles, decides whether to keep or end each green, and acts through TraCI. Then SUMO moves the traffic forward one step.

slides.title: Watch the corridor

slides.title: A camera is not perfect
slides.notes: The virtual camera has the flaws of real computer vision: limited range, missed detections that grow with distance, cars hidden behind other cars, position noise, and guessing which lane a car is in.

slides.notes: On five seeds the twin never saw, both twins beat SUMO's actuated signals at high demand, about ninety-five seconds of lost time per trip against one hundred and one. At low and medium demand, actuated control was slightly better.

slides.title: What we learned
slides.notes: The lesson is to measure, not assume. The twin always reduced stops, but cut delay only when the corridor was busy. Camera detection fell from eighty-four to fifty-six percent as queues grew. Both sensing and decision logic limit a twin.

title: Road and bridge asset twins
goals: Describe the data and models behind an asset twin
Explain condition indices, deterioration models and structural monitoring
Link a twin to maintenance decisions and lifecycle cost
reading:
What an asset twin holds

An infrastructure asset twin combines four kinds of information: geometry and design (as-built BIM in IFC 4.3, survey point clouds), condition data (inspections, automated surveys, sensors), loading and environment (traffic, axle loads, temperature, water), and history (construction, repairs). Its job is to predict future condition and support maintenance and investment decisions.

Pavements

Network surveys measure roughness as the International Roughness Index (IRI, in m/km), plus cracking, rutting and texture, often from instrumented vehicles. Condition indices such as the Pavement Condition Index (PCI) summarise distress. Deterioration is modelled statistically (regression, Markov transition matrices between condition states) or mechanistically, for example with AASHTOWare Pavement ME for design. Even ordinary vehicles' accelerometers and phones are being used to estimate roughness at scale.

Bridges and tunnels

Structural health monitoring uses strain gauges, accelerometers, displacement sensors, fibre-optic sensing and inclinometers. Vibration data allows modal analysis: changes in natural frequencies can indicate loss of stiffness. A finite-element model (OpenSees, ANSYS, Abaqus) can be updated to match measured behaviour, creating a calibrated structural twin that estimates capacity under current loads. Visual inspections remain essential; drones and image-based crack detection make them faster and safer.

From condition to decisions

DecisionTwin evidence
When to inspectRisk from condition trend, loading and consequences of failure
Which treatmentPredicted condition under each option
When to treatLifecycle cost: preservation early is usually cheaper than reconstruction later
Load restrictionsCalibrated structural model and measured response

Standards and practice

ISO 55000 sets the principles of asset management. IFC 4.3 carries design and as-built geometry. Agencies often connect the twin to their computerised maintenance management system (CMMS) so that recommendations become work orders. The IRF training on digital twins for roadway design and performance covers these data sources and tools for highway agencies.

Pitfalls

  • Sensors drift and fail; plan maintenance for the monitoring system itself.
  • Short records make deterioration models uncertain; report ranges.
  • A beautiful 3D model without condition data is a model, not a twin.

audio.title: Fixing the road before it breaks
audio.script:
Think about how most roads are maintained. A crew inspects on a fixed cycle, or waits for complaints, and repairs what has visibly failed. It works, but it is expensive, because by the time damage is visible, the cheap treatments are no longer possible. A thin overlay at year eight might have saved a full reconstruction at year fifteen.
An asset twin changes the timing. It holds the geometry of each road and bridge, its construction history, the traffic it carries, and a stream of condition data: roughness and cracking from survey vehicles, strain and vibration from bridge sensors, photos from drones. A deterioration model projects that condition forward, and the twin can compare treatments: do nothing, preserve now, or rebuild later.
For bridges, there is an extra layer. Engineers can build a finite-element model of the structure and tune it so that it vibrates the way the real bridge does. If the measured frequencies start to drift, it can be a sign of lost stiffness, worth an inspection.
The twin does not replace engineers or inspectors. It tells them where to look first and when to act. And it needs care itself: sensors drift, records are short, and predictions carry uncertainty. Report ranges, not single numbers, and link every recommendation to cost and risk, as the asset management standard ISO 55000 asks.

slides.title: An asset twin
slides.notes: An asset twin combines geometry from surveys and BIM, data from sensors and inspections, and a condition history. A deterioration model predicts the future condition, and the twin turns that into work orders.

slides.title: Measuring condition
slides.notes: Pavement condition is measured as roughness, cracking and rutting. Bridges are monitored with strain gauges, accelerometers and inspections. Drones and computer vision now find cracks faster than walking inspections.

slides.title: Predicting deterioration
slides.notes: To predict deterioration, network-level twins use statistical and Markov models. Pavement design uses mechanistic models. For a critical bridge, a finite-element model can be updated with measured vibrations to track its stiffness.

slides.title: Decisions
slides.notes: Without a twin, agencies inspect on fixed cycles and repair when damage is visible. With a twin, inspection is risk-based and repair can be timed at the lowest lifecycle cost, before expensive failure.

slides.title: Key standard
slides.notes: The asset management standard ISO 55000 frames all of this: decisions about assets should be linked to value, risk and cost over the whole lifecycle. The twin provides the evidence.

title: Urban freight and last-mile logistics
goals: Explain the pressures of on-demand and last-mile delivery
Model curbs, loading zones, micro-hubs and delivery routes
Use living labs to test freight policies with a twin
reading:
Why freight needs twins

E-commerce and on-demand services have multiplied small deliveries. Vans stop where they can, often in traffic or bus lanes; couriers circle for space; emissions and noise concentrate in residential streets. Cities have few tools to see this activity, because it is spread across many private operators who rarely share data.

What a freight twin represents

  • Supply: streets, curbs, loading bays, access restrictions, hubs.
  • Demand: parcels and deliveries by area and time, from operators or estimated from land use.
  • Operations: vehicle routes, stop durations, bay occupancy, failed deliveries.
  • Impacts: delay to other traffic and buses, emissions, safety conflicts.

Models and tools

QuestionApproachTools
Best delivery toursVehicle routing problem with time windowsjsprit, Google OR-Tools
City-wide effects of a policyAgent-based simulation of carriers and receiversMATSim freight extensions
Street and curb operationsMicrosimulation of stops and baysSUMO, Vissim
Terminals, hubs and portsDiscrete-event and agent-based simulationAnyLogic

Living labs

The EU-funded LEAD project (2020–2023) developed digital twins for sustainable on-demand urban logistics, tested in living labs in six cities including Madrid, The Hague, Budapest, Lyon, Oslo and Porto. Its free online course on the Mobility Academy platform covers urban freight basics and open-source modelling tools. A living lab pairs the twin with a real pilot: the twin predicts the effect of, say, a micro-hub, the pilot measures it, and the comparison improves the twin.

Data sharing

Operators guard their data. Practical approaches include aggregated data-sharing agreements, curb-booking systems that generate data as a by-product, sensors on loading bays, and privacy-preserving methods such as federated analytics.

Measuring success

Track both operator and public outcomes: delivery time and cost, failed deliveries, bay occupancy, illegal stops, delay to buses and traffic, emissions, and conflicts with cyclists and pedestrians.

audio.title: The van in the bus lane
audio.script:
Picture a delivery driver on a narrow city street at ten in the morning. There is a loading bay, but a car is parked in it. The next legal space is two blocks away, and there are forty more parcels on the van. So the driver stops in the bus lane for three minutes. Behind them, a bus loses two minutes, and fifty passengers lose two minutes each.
Multiply that by thousands of deliveries a day and you have the urban freight problem. Nobody planned it, and nobody can see it fully, because the data sits with many private operators.
A freight twin tries to make it visible and testable. It combines fleet positions and stop durations, loading-bay occupancy from sensors or booking systems, and estimates of delivery demand by area. Routing algorithms can then plan better tours, and traffic simulation can test policies before the city paints a single line: more loading bays, bookable curb time, a micro-hub with cargo bikes, or delivery windows.
The European LEAD project tested exactly this in living labs in six cities, and published its tools and a free course. The key idea of a living lab is to pair the twin with a real trial, so each improves the other.
And when you measure success, measure the whole street: not just how fast parcels arrive, but what the deliveries cost everyone else.

title: Environment, smart city twins and decision support
goals: Estimate emissions and air quality from a traffic twin
Place mobility inside a city-scale digital twin
Design dashboards and interfaces that support decisions
reading:
Environmental twins

Transport is a major source of greenhouse gases, air pollutants and noise. A traffic twin can estimate them at link level: speeds, accelerations and vehicle mix feed an emission model; a dispersion model estimates concentrations along streets; combined with population, it gives exposure. This lets cities test low-emission zones, signal plans or speed limits for their environmental effect, not only for travel time.

Emission models

ModelWhere usedNotes
HBEFAEuropeEmission factors by vehicle type and traffic situation; SUMO's default emission classes are based on it
COPERTEuropeWidely used for national inventories
MOVESUnited StatesUS EPA model with project-level detail

The University of Florence PhD course used in this syllabus shows how traffic flow reconstruction feeds environmental applications on its Snap4City platform. Validate against monitoring stations: modelled concentrations are sensitive to background levels, weather and street geometry.

City-scale twins

City twins integrate 3D city models (CityGML, 3D Tiles), utilities, buildings, energy and mobility. Virtual Singapore built a detailed 3D model of the city-state as a platform for planning and analysis; Helsinki has published city models and explored mobility twins. The mobility part brings the most dynamic data, which makes it both valuable and demanding. Open platforms (FIWARE with NGSI-LD, Snap4City) and commercial or cloud services (ArcGIS, Bentley iTwin, Azure Digital Twins, AWS IoT TwinMaker) host such twins; CesiumJS and deck.gl render them on the web.

Designing for decisions

  • Operators need a summary of what needs attention now, a recommended action, its reason and an easy override.
  • Planners need scenario comparisons with uncertainty ranges and the assumptions listed.
  • Decision-makers and the public need clear visual stories: before and after, who benefits, who bears the costs.

Good practice: summary before detail, state encoded in shape and colour, uncertainty shown, and every recommendation explainable. Measure use and trust (for example usability scores and operator feedback), not just model accuracy.

audio.title: Who breathes the traffic?
audio.script:
Most traffic twins are built to save time. This module asks a different question: who breathes the traffic?
A traffic twin already knows a lot. It knows how many vehicles use each street, how fast they go, how often they stop and start, and what kinds of vehicles they are. Feed that into an emission model, such as HBEFA, COPERT or MOVES, and you get estimates of carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particles, street by street. Add a dispersion model and population data, and you can see which neighbourhoods are most exposed.
That changes the conversation about a project. A new signal plan might save each driver twenty seconds, and also cut stop-and-go on a street lined with schools. A low-emission zone might shift traffic, and pollution, onto a neighbouring district. A twin can show both sides before the decision is made.
At city scale, mobility becomes one layer in a larger twin, alongside buildings, energy and water. That is powerful, but only if people use it. So the last idea of this module is about interfaces. Operators need a clear summary and a recommendation with its reason. Planners need scenarios with uncertainty. The public needs a clear story of who gains and who pays.
A twin nobody uses is just an expensive model. Design for the people who decide.

slides.title: City-scale twins
slides.notes: City-scale twins combine 3D city models with live data from many sectors. Open platforms such as FIWARE and Snap4City, and cloud twin services, host them. Singapore and Helsinki are often cited examples.

slides.notes: A twin that nobody uses is just a model. Design its interfaces for each audience: the operator in the control room, the planner, and the public.

title: Safety, security, governance, implementation and research
goals: Plan a safe, secure and lawful twin deployment
Follow a step-by-step path from pilot to service
Identify open research gaps and design a study
reading:
Safety by design

A twin that acts on the real world must fail safely. Keep decisions inside a safety shell: the twin only requests actions such as “extend green” or “end green now”; the signal controller still enforces minimum greens, yellow and all-red times and conflict monitoring, and returns to its normal plan if messages stop. Run in shadow mode for weeks before closing the loop, logging every recommendation next to what actually happened.

Cyber security and privacy

  • Separate operational networks from corporate and public ones; authenticate every API; log every command.
  • Use recognised frameworks: IEC 62443 for industrial control systems and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
  • Process video at the edge and keep only detections; aggregate and anonymise movement data; follow the EU GDPR, Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law or the law that applies.

Implementation roadmap

StepDeliverableDone when
1. Use caseDecision, owner, success measures, safety rulesSigned by the system owner
2. Data auditSources, quality, access rights, gapsAgreements in place
3. ShadowLive pipeline and dashboardData trusted by operators
4. Model and validateCalibrated modelPasses criteria on held-out days and seeds
5. Human in the loopRecommendations with reasonsOperators agree on failure cases
6. Close the loopAutomated low-risk actions with fallbackMeasured benefit on matched days
7. ScaleMore sites, agencies, standardsGovernance and funding for operation

Governance, skills and money

Decide who owns each dataset and each decision, who is accountable for automated actions, and how models are versioned and approved. Budget for operation, not just the pilot: sensor maintenance, data engineering, model recalibration and training. Many pilots stall because nobody was funded to run them in year two.

Where research is going

Recent reviews identify recurring gaps: evidence that closing the loop improves outcomes (many systems are shadows); data fusion, real-time processing and standardisation; federation of twins across agencies and modes; whole-lifecycle frameworks for infrastructure; human behaviour and vulnerable road users; fidelity, uncertainty and trust; security and privacy; organisational and business models; and under-studied modes such as bus transit. Promising directions include AI surrogate models for faster-than-real-time simulation, physics-informed learning, graph neural networks, federated learning, generative scenarios for automated-vehicle testing, and V2X channels that let twins talk to vehicles directly.

Designing a study

Name the decision, the gap and the evidence; choose a method (simulation experiment, field pilot, design science, systematic review, case study); evaluate fidelity, timeliness, decision value, safety, robustness and acceptance; and report on held-out data and several seeds. The Layer 3 question builder on this site turns these choices into a draft research question.

audio.title: The pilot that nobody ran in year two
audio.script:
Many digital twin projects end the same way. The pilot is a success. There is a launch event, a video, a press release. And eighteen months later, the dashboard is still on the wall, but the data feeds have quietly stopped, the model has not been recalibrated since the road works, and the engineer who understood it has moved on.
This final module is about avoiding that ending. It has three parts.
First, safety and trust. A twin that acts on the real world must sit inside a safety shell, where the controller hardware still enforces minimum greens and fallback plans. It should run for weeks in shadow mode, recommending but not acting, so operators can see where it is wrong. And it must be secure and respect privacy, from network separation to processing video at the edge.
Second, a rollout path: one use case, a data audit, a shadow, a validated model, a human in the loop, then closing the loop for low-risk actions, and only then scaling up. And a budget for operation, not just for the launch.
Third, the frontier. Research still lacks strong evidence that closing the loop pays off, and has open questions about data fusion, trust, federation across agencies, and human behaviour. If you go on to research, name the decision, the gap and the evidence, and test on data you did not tune on.
Thank you for taking this course. Now go and build something that is still running in year two.

slides.title: From pilot to service
slides.notes: The final module is about making a twin real: keeping it safe, secure and lawful, rolling it out step by step, and knowing where research still has open questions.

slides.title: Safety and security
slides.notes: Safety comes from a shell around the twin: the signal controller keeps enforcing minimum greens, yellows and fallback plans. Cyber security follows standards such as IEC 62443 and the NIST framework. Privacy follows laws such as GDPR or Saudi Arabia's PDPL.

slides.title: Rollout
slides.notes: Roll out in steps: one use case, a data audit, a shadow with trusted live data, a validated model, a human in the loop, then closing the loop for low-risk actions, and finally scaling.

slides.title: Governance
slides.notes: Governance answers who owns the data and the decisions, who is accountable if an automated action goes wrong, and who will have the skills to run the twin after the pilot team leaves.

slides.title: Open research gaps
slides.notes: Research gaps remain. Few studies prove the value of closing the loop. Data fusion, uncertainty and trust are open problems, as are federating twins across agencies and modelling human behaviour, especially of pedestrians and cyclists.

slides.title: A good research question
slides.notes: To finish: a good research question names the decision, the gap and the evidence. And whatever you build, test it on data you did not tune on. Thank you for completing the course.
